title: IoT & CPS Protocols Explained Simply — WiFi, ZigBee, Z-Wave, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Modbus, PROFINET, M2M
description: Every protocol in the IoT & CPS protocols deck: architecture, structure, working, real-world examples and functionality.
endCard: 📘 5 headings: architecture · structure · working · examples · functionality

scenes.title: Intro
lines: Smart homes, farms, factories and cities all have machines talking to each other. But they don't all speak the same language.
Each language is a protocol. This video covers every protocol in the IoT and CPS protocols deck. CPS means cyber physical systems.
For each one, the slides give five things: its architecture, its structure, how it works, real world examples, and its functionality.
We will cover eight protocols: WiFi, ZigBee, Z-Wave, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Modbus TCP, PROFINET, and machine to machine, or M2M.
Tip: in the exam, write each protocol under exactly these five headings.

scenes.title: The five headings
lines: Architecture is the shape of the network. Star means everyone talks to one centre. Mesh means devices pass messages through each other.
Structure tells you the layers: the radio frequency and physical layer, the MAC or data link layer, and the application layer.
Working is the step by step journey of the data.
Applications are real products that use it.
And functionality is the protocol's main strengths. Now, protocol one.

scenes.title: 1. WiFi (IEEE 802.11)
lines: WiFi, also called IEEE 802.11. You use it every day.
Architecture: star topology. Devices connect to an Access Point, which connects to the local network, and then to the internet.
Structure: the physical layer uses two point four or five gigahertz. The data link layer is the IEEE 802.11 MAC. On top runs the normal TCP/IP stack.
Working, step one: the device scans for available networks.
Step two: it associates with the Access Point. Associate simply means joins.
Step three: data is exchanged using TCP/IP.
Step four: the Access Point forwards the data to the router and the internet.
Examples: a smart home speaker like Amazon Echo communicates with the cloud over WiFi.
And industrial PCs send data from machines to a cloud dashboard.
Functionality: high bandwidth, it supports mobility, and it is suitable for a local area.

scenes.title: 2. ZigBee (IEEE 802.15.4)
lines: Protocol two: ZigBee, which is built on IEEE 802.15.4.
Architecture: it supports mesh, star and tree topologies. Sensors and actuators send to a Coordinator, then a Home Hub, then the Cloud.
Structure: the physical layer uses two point four gigahertz, or eight sixty eight or nine fifteen megahertz.
The MAC layer is IEEE 802.15.4, and the application layer is the ZigBee Cluster Library.
Working, step one: sensors detect events, like motion or a door opening.
Step two: the data is sent to the Coordinator.
Step three: it is aggregated, meaning collected together, at the Hub.
Step four: it is communicated to the cloud.
Examples: the Philips Hue lighting system for home automation.
And soil moisture sensors that report data for precision irrigation.
Functionality: low power operation and reliable mesh networking. If one path fails, messages hop through another device.

scenes.title: 3. Z-Wave
lines: Protocol three: Z-Wave, another smart home protocol.
Architecture: mesh topology. Devices connect to a Z-Wave Controller, which connects to the cloud or a mobile app.
Structure: it uses sub gigahertz frequencies, around nine oh eight or eight sixty eight megahertz.
And it uses a proprietary stack. Proprietary means owned by one company, not an open standard.
Working, step one: a sensor or actuator sends data to the Controller.
Step two: the Controller forwards commands back to devices.
Step three: repeaters extend coverage. Powered devices relay messages for devices that are far away.
Examples: Yale smart locks that you can control remotely.
And smart thermostats adjusting home temperature.
Functionality: low power, simple device pairing, and interoperable, meaning devices from different brands work together.

scenes.title: 4. LoRaWAN
lines: Protocol four: LoRaWAN. Long range wide area network.
Architecture: star of stars. End devices send to gateways, gateways send to a Network Server, which sends to an Application Server.
Star of stars means each gateway is the centre of its own star, and all gateways together form a bigger star around the server.
Structure: sub gigahertz, eight sixty eight or nine fifteen megahertz, with the LoRaWAN protocol stack.
Working, step one: the sensor sends data using LoRa radio.
Step two: the gateway forwards it to the Network Server.
Step three: the server processes it and forwards it to the Application Server.
Examples: soil moisture sensors in a farm sending data for irrigation.
And LoRaWAN tags for tracking shipping containers.
Functionality: long range, very low power, and suitable for sparse sensor networks, where devices are few and far apart.

scenes.title: 5. NB-IoT
lines: Protocol five: NB-IoT, narrowband IoT, which runs on mobile networks.
Architecture: star topology. The IoT device talks to a Base Station, which connects to the Core Network, and then to the Cloud Application.
Structure: it uses the LTE spectrum, but only narrowband resource blocks. A resource block is a small slice of the LTE channel.
Working, step one: the device connects to the NB-IoT base station.
Step two: data is sent using minimal LTE resources.
Step three: it is forwarded to the cloud.
Examples: smart meters sending consumption data.
And parking sensors sending whether a parking slot is free.
Functionality: low power, deep coverage, even underground, and cost effective.

scenes.title: 6. Modbus TCP
lines: Protocol six: Modbus TCP, used in factories.
Architecture: a client server model, also called master and slave. The master asks, the slaves answer.
In Modbus TCP, the master is the client, and each slave device acts as a server.
Structure: the physical layer is Ethernet, and the application layer is Modbus commands.
Working, step one: the master sends read or write requests. For example, read register ten.
Step two: the slave responds with the data.
Step three: all this communication happens over TCP/IP.
Examples: temperature sensors in a chemical plant reporting to a PLC, a programmable logic controller.
And HVAC system controllers reading thermostats. HVAC means heating, ventilation and air conditioning.
Functionality: simple, built for industrial communication, and reliable for data and control.

scenes.title: 7. PROFINET
lines: Protocol seven: PROFINET, an industrial Ethernet protocol.
Architecture: industrial Ethernet, connecting controllers to field devices. Field devices are the machines on the factory floor.
Structure: Ethernet at the physical layer, with deterministic data exchange.
Deterministic means the timing is guaranteed. A message always arrives within a fixed time. That's critical when a robot is moving.
Working, step one: PLCs send real time commands.
Step two: field devices respond deterministically, always on time.
Think of it like a train timetable. Every message has a fixed slot, so nothing is ever late.
Step three: the system handles diagnostics, detecting faults and problems.
Examples: a robotic arm in a car assembly line.
And process monitoring in chemical plants.
Functionality: high speed, deterministic control, and it supports redundancy, meaning backup paths if one link fails.

scenes.title: 8. M2M (Machine-to-Machine)
lines: Protocol eight: M2M, machine to machine. Machines talk to each other with no human in between.
Architecture: either peer to peer, or client server. A sensor or actuator talks to a cloud server, or directly to a peer device.
Peer to peer means two equal devices talk directly. Client server means one central server.
Structure: M2M is a concept, so it uses existing protocols, for example MQTT, CoAP, HTTP, Modbus, or NB-IoT.
Working, step one: the sensor collects data.
Step two: the data is packaged, in a format like JSON or XML.
Step three: it is sent via a protocol to the server or peer.
Step four: the server responds with commands. For example, send a refill truck.
Examples: vending machine stock monitoring.
And remote oil pump monitoring, in places where no engineer is around.
Functionality: automated communication, scalable to thousands of machines, and ideal for remote monitoring.

scenes.title: Comparison table
lines: Let's compare all eight. WiFi: star topology, two point four or five gigahertz, best for high bandwidth.
ZigBee: mesh, star or tree, on 802.15.4, best for low power mesh networks.
Z-Wave: mesh, sub gigahertz, proprietary, with simple pairing.
LoRaWAN: star of stars, sub gigahertz, long range and very low power.
NB-IoT: star, on the LTE spectrum, with deep coverage.
Modbus TCP: master and slave over Ethernet, simple and reliable.
PROFINET: industrial Ethernet with deterministic, guaranteed timing.
And M2M: peer to peer or client server, using protocols like MQTT and CoAP.

scenes.title: How to pick one
lines: To finish, a quick way to remember them. In a smart home, use ZigBee or Z-Wave for low power mesh, or WiFi for high bandwidth.
On a farm or wide area with few sensors, use LoRaWAN.
For city meters and parking sensors, NB-IoT, because it uses the existing mobile network.
For simple factory sensors, Modbus TCP.
For real time robots, PROFINET.
And for machines reporting automatically from far away, M2M. Remember the five headings for each, and you're ready!
